title: How can you use AI to create training content safely?
seoTitle: Using AI to create training safely
description: Safe workflow for AI assisted training content: approved tools, clean source packs, outcomes first, grounded drafts, claim checks, expert review, provenance.
shortAnswer: To use AI to create training content safely, treat it as a drafting assistant inside a controlled workflow. Use only approved tools, keep personal and confidential information out of public tools, define learning outcomes before prompting, ground drafts in approved and current source documents, and have a qualified person check every factual claim against its source. Record the tool, sources, reviewer, and approval for each item before release.
keyTakeaways: Generative AI produces fluent text that can be wrong. Every factual claim in a draft needs checking against an approved source by someone qualified to judge it.

Privacy regulators warn against feeding personal information into public AI tools. For example, the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) recommends not entering personal information, particularly sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools.
AI is well suited to restructuring approved material, drafting scenarios, and writing distractors. It is poorly suited to stating thresholds, dates, penalties, or legal requirements from memory.
Defining outcomes and assessment points first gives the AI a structure to fill and gives reviewers a standard to check against.
A provenance record for each item (tool, sources, reviewer, approval) is what makes AI assisted content defensible later.

sections.heading: What are the risks of using AI to write training content?

blocks.text: The main risks are confident but inaccurate content, disclosure of personal or confidential information, material that reflects the wrong jurisdiction or an outdated rule, and the loss of any record of where a statement came from. In regulated training these risks compound, because a wrong statement is taught to many people and then assessed as correct.

Privacy regulators have drawn out the same risk. For example, the OAIC notes that generative AI is "probabilistic in nature and does not 'understand' the data it handles or generates", and that inferred or artificially generated information about an identifiable person, including hallucinations, is personal information that must be handled under the Australian Privacy Principles ([OAIC](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/guidance-on-privacy-and-the-use-of-commercially-available-ai-products)). For training teams, the practical consequence is simple: a draft is a hypothesis until someone checks it.

This guide covers the creation workflow for a piece of content. The organizational controls that sit around it, such as the tool register, accountability, monitoring, and periodic review, are covered in [how to govern AI generated learning content](/guides/how-to-govern-ai-generated-learning-content).

sections.heading: Which parts of training development suit AI?

blocks.text: AI helps most where the facts are already fixed in an approved source and the task is to restructure, rephrase, or generate variations. It helps least where the task is to supply facts, because that is where fabrication does the most damage.

sections.heading: What is a safe workflow for AI assisted content creation?

blocks.text: A safe workflow fixes the inputs, constrains the generation, checks the outputs, and records what happened. Each step below produces an output that the next step or a later audit relies on.

items: **Confirm the tool and use are approved.** Check the tool is on your organization's approved list and that content drafting is a permitted use. Output: a reference to the approved tool and use case in your AI register.

**Assemble a source pack.** Collect the current, approved documents the content must reflect, with version numbers. Remove personal information and anything the tool's terms do not allow. Output: a versioned source pack.

**Define outcomes and assessment points first.** Write the [learning outcomes](/guides/how-to-write-measurable-learning-outcomes) and what evidence will show each one. Output: an outcome and assessment list that the draft must satisfy.

**Generate grounded drafts.** Instruct the tool to use only the source pack, to mark which source passage supports each statement, and to flag gaps rather than fill them. Output: a draft with source markers.
**Check every claim.** A reviewer compares each factual statement with the cited passage and marks it confirmed, corrected, or removed. Output: a claim check log.

**Expert and compliance review.** A subject matter expert confirms scenarios, model answers, and emphasis; compliance or legal review applies where the content implements an obligation. Output: a signed review record.
**Accessibility and fairness review.** Check reading level, alternative text, and whether names, examples, or scenarios introduce bias or stereotypes. Output: review notes and fixes.
**Record provenance and approve.** Record the tool and version, date, source pack version, reviewers, and approver against the content item. Output: an approved item with a provenance record.
**Hand over to maintenance.** Register the item's source dependencies so a change to a source triggers review. Output: a review trigger in the content system.

sections.heading: What privacy rules apply when using AI tools for training content?

blocks.text: Privacy law applies to any personal information you put into an AI tool and to any personal information it produces, so check the privacy rules in each jurisdiction where you operate. For example, under Australia's Privacy Act 1988, the OAIC recommends as a matter of best practice that organizations "do not enter personal information, and particularly sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools" ([OAIC](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/guidance-on-privacy-and-the-use-of-commercially-available-ai-products)). The points below follow that guidance; most privacy regimes raise similar questions.

items: **Case material.** Incident reports, complaints, and investigation files often contain personal information. De-identify them before use, or write fictional cases based on the pattern.
**Use and disclosure.** Under APP 6, personal information entered into an AI system may only be used or disclosed for the purpose it was collected for, unless consent or an exception applies.
**Accuracy.** APP 10 requires reasonable steps to ensure accuracy, and the OAIC says those steps should be commensurate with the increased risk in an AI context.

**Due diligence.** Before adopting a commercial tool, the OAIC suggests checking whether it has been tested for the intended use, how human oversight can be built in, and who can access information entered into it.

blocks.text: Government bodies and other organizations covered by security frameworks should also check whether those frameworks require an AI usage policy, and make sure content drafting sits within it. See also [privacy training requirements](/regulations/privacy-act-staff-training-requirements).

sections.heading: What should you check before releasing AI assisted content?

blocks.text: Before release, confirm that the inputs were approved, every claim was checked, qualified people reviewed the content, and the record is complete. The checklist below can be used as a release gate.

blocks.title: Release checklist for AI assisted training content
blocks.text: Tool and use case are approved and recorded. Source pack is current and versioned. No personal or confidential information was entered contrary to policy. Outcomes and assessment points were defined before drafting. Every factual statement is confirmed against a source, corrected, or removed. Thresholds, dates, penalties, and clause numbers were taken from primary sources, not from the tool. Subject matter expert and, where relevant, compliance review are signed. Accessibility and fairness review is complete. Provenance record is attached to the item. Source dependencies are registered for future review.

Australia's [Guidance for AI Adoption](https://www.ai.gov.au/staying-safe-and-responsible/essential-ai-practices/guidance-ai-adoption-foundations) published by the National Artificial Intelligence Centre recommends matching human oversight to how much autonomy a system has and how high the stakes are, with mandatory human review for high stakes decisions. Training that people rely on to meet legal obligations sits at the high stakes end.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry defines the knowledge framework (concepts, outcomes, assessment points, and their sources) before any content is generated, so AI assisted drafting fills a reviewed structure rather than inventing one. Each statement keeps its provenance to the source passage, and human verification is recorded before release. The [verification and trust](/platform/verification-trust) page describes these controls.

faqs.q: Do learners need to be told that content was drafted with AI?
faqs.a: It depends on the context and your own AI policy. The Guidance for AI Adoption recommends communicating AI use as standard practice, especially where AI generates content that can meaningfully affect people. Many organizations note AI assistance in the content record and disclose it where learners interact with AI directly, such as a chatbot tutor.

faqs.q: Can we paste our internal policies into a public AI chatbot?
faqs.a: Check your AI usage policy and the tool's terms first. Internal policies may be confidential, and many contain names or contact details. The OAIC recommends against entering personal information into publicly available generative AI tools. An approved enterprise tool with appropriate data handling terms is the safer option.

faqs.q: Does AI assistance reduce the review effort?
faqs.a: It usually shifts effort rather than removing it. Drafting becomes faster, but checking becomes more important, because fluent text hides errors. Teams that plan review time for statement level checks get the speed benefit without accepting the accuracy risk.

Yes, with review. AI is good at generating variations and plausible distractors. A subject matter expert must confirm that the keyed answer is correct, that distractors are wrong for a clear reason, and that each item tests the intended outcome rather than reading skill or trick wording.

factCheck.claim: OAIC recommends, as a matter of best practice, that organisations do not enter personal information, and particularly sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools. Guidance published 21 October 2024, updated 17 January 2025.

OAIC: under APP 10 organisations must take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information, commensurate with the increased risk in an AI context; AI generated or inferred information about an identifiable individual is personal information.

OAIC: if personal information is input into an AI system, APP 6 requires it only be used or disclosed for the primary purpose of collection unless consent or an exception applies; due diligence should consider how human oversight can be embedded.

Guidance for AI adoption foundations: make it standard practice to communicate AI use, especially where AI generates content that can meaningfully impact people; match oversight to autonomy and stakes, with mandatory human review for high-stakes decisions.

The six essential practices: decide who is accountable; understand impacts and plan accordingly; measure and manage risks; share essential information; test and monitor; maintain human control. Practice 4.1 is maintaining an AI register.
